q1.answer: For most teams, no, but it gets oversold as a fix for everything. I'd lean on it when answers must cite your own documents, and skip it when the real problem is an unclear task.

q2.answer: I'd contain it first by narrowing what the feature is allowed to answer, then write the failure as a test case before touching the prompt. The test is what keeps it from coming back.

q3.answer: Not entirely. I'd let it handle routine, well-defined questions and send anything ambiguous or emotional to a person, then watch where people escalate to decide what to automate next.

q4.answer: I'd be cautious. My instinct is to give an agent narrow, reversible actions first and widen its reach only as evals show it behaves, because trust should be earned in steps.

q5.answer: I start from the cost of a wrong answer. Where a mistake is expensive or can't be undone, I'd have it refuse or hand off to a person, and I'd test those cases before anything else.

q6.answer: Failure modes first. I'd list the specific ways it can go wrong, write a pass or fail check for each, and use code wherever code can decide before reaching for an AI judge.

q7.answer: Accuracy first. A note taker that is wrong loses trust faster than a missing feature gains it. I'd measure accuracy on real meetings, fix the worst failure modes, and add features once people stop correcting the notes.

q8.answer: Shipping before they can say how they'd know it failed. I'd write the failure cases and the checks first, then build, so quality is something you measure instead of hope for.

q9.answer: I'd spend it on the one workflow where a wrong answer is cheapest to catch and most valuable to get right, and cut everything else. Breadth can wait. I'd rather have one feature measured and trusted than five that nobody can vouch for.

q10.answer: Later than most teams think. I'd push prompting and evals as far as they go first, because they are cheap and reversible, and fine-tune only when a measured gap remains that prompting cannot close.

q11.answer: I'd get them to agree on how failure is defined before anyone argues about the design. Once the pass or fail checks are written down, the debate becomes about evidence instead of opinions.

q12.answer: Start with one real workflow the team already does and make it measurably better with AI, instead of teaching tools in the abstract. People adopt what visibly saves them time, so I'd pick the first win carefully and teach from there.

q13.answer: They forget the human side. Most offices, even very large ones, still run on spreadsheets and email, so the real opportunity is often a simple problem people have every day, not something cutting edge.

q14.answer: No, and I'm proudest of the calls where I'd choose not to use it. Plenty of problems don't need robust intelligence, and a deterministic system often wins.

q15.answer: When it isn't necessary, when it would be immoral, or when it risks long-term harm to the customers. If any of those is true, I'd walk away from the AI version.

q16.answer: I follow a few sources I trust and deliberately avoid too many Silicon Valley voices, because it turns into circular thinking. I'd rather listen to researchers and to the people actually doing the work.

q17.answer: Mostly by listening. People want to be heard and understood, and once they are, getting everyone singing from the same songbook is much easier.

q18.answer: Ambiguous ones with no track record of success. I like charting new territory, where nobody can tell you the answer in advance.
